items.hint1: The instruction asks for a word nearly opposite to the underlined word that also fits the gap. First work out what the underlined word means. The word 'while' tells you the two halves of the sentence are in contrast.
items.hint2: Malevolence means wishing harm or evil on other people. Any option that also means harm, cruelty or unfriendliness is a synonym, not an opposite, so set it aside.
items.hint3: Two options remain: indifference and benevolence. A true opposite sits at the other extreme, not in the middle. Which of the two does that?
items.solution:
Answer: B. benevolence

An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning. Malevolence is the wish to do harm to others, so its opposite is the wish to do good to others, which is benevolence. It also fits the hero, whose goodness showed in his deeds.

How to tell: the word roots help. 'Mal-' means bad, as in malpractice, and 'bene-' means good, as in benefit and benefactor. The word 'while' sets the hero against the villain, so the gap needs a good quality.

Why not the others:
A. wickedness: this means the same as malevolence, so it is a synonym.
C. indifference: this means not caring either way, which is a middle point, not the opposite of wishing harm.
D. hostility: this means unfriendliness or ill feeling, which is close to malevolence.

Exam tip: in antonym questions, first cross out every option that means the same as the underlined word. Then choose the word at the other extreme, not a neutral middle word.

items.hint1: Work out what the underlined phrase means, then look for a word that describes the opposite kind of event. The word 'while' marks the contrast.
items.hint2: An august occasion is grand, dignified and important, like a coronation, when a king or queen is crowned. 'Grand' means almost exactly the same, so it cannot be the opposite.
items.hint3: Of solemn, trivial and ceremonious, two words keep the idea of seriousness or formality. Which one does not?
items.solution:
Answer: C. trivial

As an adjective, 'august' (said au-GUST) means grand, dignified and deserving respect. Its opposite is something small and unimportant, which is what 'trivial' means.

How to tell: the sentence contrasts a coronation, the crowning of a king or queen, with a small office party. The gap needs a word for an ordinary, unimportant event, the opposite of august.

Why not the others:
A. grand: this means the same as august, so it is a synonym.
B. solemn: this means serious and dignified, which is close to august.
D. ceremonious: this means formal and full of ceremony, which suits a coronation, not the opposite of it.

Exam tip: some familiar words have a second meaning as adjectives. When the underlined word does not fit its usual sense, as with 'august', read the sentence around it to find the meaning being used.

items.hint1: Work out what the underlined word means, then find its opposite. The word 'but' tells you the rivals behaved differently from the team.
items.hint2: Being complacent means feeling so pleased with yourself that you stop trying hard and stop watching for danger. Words meaning 'pleased' or 'satisfied' are close to complacent, not opposite to it.
items.hint3: That leaves vigilant and indifferent. One is close to not caring; the other is the opposite of relaxing your guard. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: B. vigilant

Complacent describes someone so satisfied with past success that they relax and stop watching for problems. The opposite is to stay watchful and alert, which is what 'vigilant' means.

How to tell: 'but' sets the rivals against the team. The team relaxed after early success, so the rivals did the opposite and stayed careful all season.

Why not the others:
A. content: this means pleased or satisfied, which is close to complacent.
C. satisfied: this is part of the meaning of complacent, so it is a near-synonym.
D. indifferent: this means not caring, which is close to the relaxed attitude of a complacent team, not its opposite.

Exam tip: link each word to a picture of behaviour. Complacent is a team relaxing after a win; its opposite is a team still on guard. Choose the option that shows the opposite behaviour.

items.hint1: Find the meaning of the underlined word, then its opposite. The words 'but' and 'actually' show that the records turned out different from the claims.
items.hint2: Bogus means fake or not real. Words meaning dishonest, false or misleading are synonyms of it.
items.hint3: Three of the options are about falseness or trickery. Test each one: does it mean fake, or does it mean the opposite?
items.solution:
Answer: C. genuine

Bogus means fake or false. Its opposite is real and true, which is what 'genuine' means.

How to tell: 'but ... actually' signals a surprise. The claims were fake, yet the financial records turned out to be real, so the gap needs a word for real.

Why not the others:
A. fraudulent: this means dishonest and meant to cheat, so it is a synonym of bogus.
B. deceptive: this means misleading, which is close to bogus.
D. counterfeit: this means a fake copy, as with false money, so it is a synonym.

Exam tip: when three options share one idea and one option stands apart, the odd one out is often the antonym. Check it against the underlined word before you choose.

items.hint1: Work out what kind of person the underlined word describes, then look for the opposite quality. The word 'while' shows the assistant was different.
items.hint2: A quick-tempered person gets angry fast. Irritable and volatile both describe someone easily upset, so they are close to it, not opposite.
items.hint3: Between impulsive and patient, which one is the opposite of flaring up quickly when things get hard?
items.solution:
Answer: B. patient

A quick-tempered person becomes angry very quickly. The opposite is someone who stays calm and can put up with trouble without getting angry, and that is a patient person.

How to tell: 'while' contrasts the man who shouted at employees with his assistant. 'In stressful situations' shows the assistant kept calm when things were hard.

Why not the others:
A. irritable: this means easily annoyed, so it is a synonym.
C. impulsive: this means acting suddenly without thinking, which is close to losing your temper, not its opposite.
D. volatile: this means likely to change mood or explode suddenly, so it is a synonym.

Exam tip: for a word describing character, ask how that person behaves under pressure. The antonym describes the opposite behaviour in the same situation.

items.hint1: The underlined word describes when an animal is active. Find the word for the opposite time.
items.hint2: Nocturnal means active at night. An option that also means active at night, or one that only describes feeling tired, is not its opposite.
items.hint3: You are left with crepuscular and diurnal. One of them refers to twilight, the half-light at dawn and dusk. Which time of day is the full opposite of night?
items.solution:
Answer: B. diurnal

Nocturnal animals are active at night and rest by day. Animals that do the opposite, active by day and resting at night, are called diurnal. Most owls hunt at night, while eagles hunt by day.

How to tell: 'unlike' tells you the eagle differs from the owl, so the gap needs the daytime word. A memory aid: 'diurnal' comes from the Latin word for day, like 'diary', a record kept day by day.

Why not the others:
A. crepuscular: this means active at twilight, around dawn and dusk, which is neither the full opposite nor the eagle's habit.
C. night-active: this means the same as nocturnal, so it is a synonym.
D. sleepy: this describes feeling tired, not the time of day an animal is active.

Exam tip: learn opposites in pairs, such as nocturnal and diurnal, or ascend and descend. Examiners often test one word of a pair by asking for the other.

items.hint1: This set asks for a word nearly the same in meaning as the key word, here 'repealed'. The word 'similarly' tells you the second action matched the first.
items.hint2: To repeal a law is to cancel it officially. Words about making a law, applying it or keeping it in force go the other way.
items.hint3: Enacted and enforced are both about putting a law into action. Of revoked and sustained, which one matches cancelling?
items.solution:
Answer: B. revoked

A synonym is a word with the same or nearly the same meaning. To repeal a law is to cancel it officially, and to revoke a rule is also to cancel it officially, so the two are synonyms.

How to tell: 'similarly' means 'in the same way'. The law was cancelled last month, so the old regulation was cancelled this week as well.

Why not the others:
A. enacted: this means made into law, the opposite of repealed.
C. enforced: this means put into action so that people must obey it, not cancelled.
D. sustained: this means kept going or upheld, the opposite of cancelled.

Exam tip: linking words set the relation. 'Similarly', 'equally' and 'likewise' call for a word with the same meaning; 'but', 'while' and 'unlike' usually call for an opposite.

items.hint1: Find the meaning of the underlined word. 'Equally surprising' tells you his behaviour was the same kind of thing as hers.
items.hint2: Impertinence means rudeness or lack of respect, especially towards someone older or more senior. Any option that means good manners or respect is its opposite.
items.hint3: After removing the polite words, you have insolence and timidity. Which one would shock a meeting in the same way rudeness does?
items.solution:
Answer: C. insolence

Impertinence is rude, disrespectful behaviour. Insolence also means rude and disrespectful behaviour, so the two are synonyms.

How to tell: 'equally surprising' shows his behaviour matched hers. Her impertinence shocked everyone, so his behaviour was the same kind: rude and disrespectful.

Why not the others:
A. politeness: this means good manners, the opposite of impertinence.
B. deference: this means polite respect for someone senior, also the opposite.
D. timidity: this means shyness or lack of courage, which is a different quality, not rudeness.

Exam tip: when the options include words on both sides of a meaning, such as rudeness and respect, remove the side that goes the wrong way first. Then check the words that are left against the marked word.

items.hint1: Work out what the underlined word means. The sentence tells you the villagers respected it and went to the elder for it.
items.hint2: Sagacity means sound judgement and good sense, the quality of a wise person. Foolishness and ignorance go the other way, so rule them out.
items.hint3: You are left with wisdom and knowledge. Knowing many facts and judging well are not quite the same thing. Which one is sagacity?
items.solution:
Answer: C. wisdom

Sagacity is the ability to judge well and give good advice. That is wisdom, so wisdom is the synonym. A memory aid: a sage, a wise person, sounds like the start of sagacity.

How to tell: people go to an elder on important matters for good judgement, and 'sought his wisdom' says exactly that.

Why not the others:
A. foolishness: this is lack of good sense, the opposite.
B. ignorance: this is lack of knowledge, which is on the opposite side.
D. knowledge: this is knowing facts. A person can know a lot and still judge badly, so it is related to sagacity but not the same.

Exam tip: when two options look close, ask which one matches the marked word exactly, not just roughly. Examiners often place a related word beside the true synonym.

items.hint1: The set asks for a word nearly the same in meaning as the underlined word. 'Similarly' tells you the security system was thought to be like the fortress.
items.hint2: Impregnable means so strong that it cannot be broken into or captured. Words meaning weak or easy to get into are opposites.
items.hint3: Compare vulnerable and invulnerable. The prefix 'in-' often means 'not'. Which of the two describes something that cannot be attacked successfully?
items.solution:
Answer: D. invulnerable

Impregnable means impossible to break into or capture. Invulnerable means impossible to harm or damage, so the two are synonyms.

How to tell: 'similarly' shows the security system was thought to be as strong as the fortress. Here the prefix 'in-' means 'not', so invulnerable means 'not vulnerable', not open to attack.

Why not the others:
A. vulnerable: this means open to attack or harm, the opposite.
B. weak: this means lacking strength, the opposite.
C. accessible: this means easy to get into, the opposite.

Exam tip: do not guess a meaning from a word the marked word looks like. Impregnable has nothing to do with pregnancy. Use the sentence instead: a fortress and a security system both exist to keep people out.

items.hint1: The underlined word describes how often something happens. The word 'and' links rain and snow in the same way.
items.hint2: Seldom means not often. Frequently and regularly describe things that happen often, so rule them out.
items.hint3: You are left with occasionally and rarely. Both describe things that do not happen all the time. Which one stresses how uncommon the event is, as seldom does?
items.solution:
Answer: C. rarely

Seldom means hardly ever. Rarely means the same, so it is the synonym. In a desert, rain hardly ever falls, and snow even less.

How to tell: put the option in place of the marked word. 'Rain rarely falls' says exactly what 'Rain seldom falls' says, and 'snowfall rarely occurs' keeps the same idea.

Why not the others:
A. frequently: this means often, the opposite.
B. occasionally: this means now and then, which suggests the event happens from time to time; it does not stress how uncommon it is.
D. regularly: this means at steady, frequent intervals, the opposite.

Exam tip: for words of frequency, picture a scale: always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, seldom or rarely, never. The synonym is the word at the same point on the scale.

items.hint1: Find the meaning of the underlined word. 'Equally' tells you the shower had the same effect as the run.
items.hint2: Invigorating means filling you with energy and making you feel lively. Look for the option that describes the same good effect.
items.hint3: Three options describe much the same effect as each other. Is that effect the one invigorating describes, or its opposite?
items.solution:
Answer: C. refreshing

Something invigorating gives you new energy and makes you feel lively. Something refreshing does the same, so the two are synonyms. The word 'vigour' inside invigorating means energy and strength.

How to tell: 'equally' means 'in the same way', so the shower had the same effect as the run: it made the person feel fresh and full of energy.

Why not the others:
A. exhausting: this means using up all your energy, the opposite.
B. draining: this means taking your energy away, the opposite.
D. tiring: this means making you feel tired, the opposite.

Exam tip: look for a smaller word inside a long one, such as vigour in invigorating or courage in encourage. It often points to the meaning.

items.hint1: The gap is the verb, and it must agree with its subject in number. Look at how the subject is built: two nouns joined by a pair of linking words.
items.hint2: With 'neither ... nor' and 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the noun closer to it. Find which noun sits next to the gap and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.hint3: The nearer noun is plural, so a singular verb is out. Among the plural forms, look for any word that points to the past or to a period up to now. If there is none, which form suits a plain statement about the present?
items.solution:
Answer: B. are

When two subjects are joined by 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. This is called the rule of proximity, which means nearness.

How to tell:
The nearer subject is 'the teachers', which is plural.
So the verb must be plural: 'are', not 'is'.
The sentence has no past-time word such as 'last year' or 'then', so the simple present fits: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers are satisfied.'

Why not the others:
A. is: this agrees with 'the principal', which is the farther subject.
C. were: this is plural but past tense, and nothing in the sentence points to the past.
D. have been: this adds the idea of 'up to now', and no word in the sentence calls for it.

Exam tip: in 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor' sentences, cover the first subject with your finger and make the verb agree with the one that is left.

items.hint1: The subject is a collective noun, a single word for a group of people. Decide whether the sentence treats the group as one unit or as separate members.
items.hint2: In the grammar taught for this exam, a collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one body, and a plural verb when the members act or think separately. Look at what 'divided on the issue' says about the members.
items.hint3: Ask yourself: can a group be divided if its members all think as one? Decide on singular or plural, then check the remaining options for any tense clue in the sentence.
items.solution:
Answer: A. are

In the grammar taught for UTME, a collective noun such as committee, jury, team or family takes a plural verb when its members are thought of as acting or feeling separately, and a singular verb when the group acts as one unit.

How to tell: 'divided on the issue' means the members hold different views from one another. The committee is not acting as one body, so the plural is used: 'The committee are divided.' Compare 'The committee is meeting today', where the group acts together.

Why not the others:
B. is: this treats the committee as one united body, which clashes with the idea of being divided. Many American writers would use it, but it is not the form this exam tests here.
C. were: this is plural but past tense, and nothing in the sentence points to the past.
D. have been: this adds the idea of 'up to now', and no word in the sentence calls for it.

Exam tip: with a collective noun, look for a word showing the members disagree or act separately, such as divided, disagree, quarrel or went to their homes. If you find one, choose the plural verb.

items.hint1: The verb must agree with its subject. Here the subject is a phrase: an expression of amount followed by a noun. Decide which word in it controls the verb.
items.hint2: Expressions like 'a number of' and 'a variety of' followed by a plural noun work like the word 'many' or 'various'. In the grammar taught for this exam, the verb then agrees with the plural noun after 'of'.
items.hint3: The noun after 'of' is plural, so the singular forms drop out. Is the sentence about the past, or about what can be chosen now?
items.solution:
Answer: B. are

In the grammar taught for UTME, 'a variety of' followed by a plural noun means 'various' or 'many different', so the verb agrees with that plural noun, just as it does after 'a number of'.

How to tell:
The noun after 'of' is 'options', which is plural.
'A variety of options' means 'various options', so the verb is plural: 'are'.
Nothing in the sentence points to the past, so the present form fits.

Why not the others:
A. is: this treats 'variety' as the subject. Some grammar books accept it, but it is not the pattern this exam tests.
C. was: this is singular and past tense.
D. were: this is plural but past tense, and no word in the sentence points to the past.

Exam tip: compare 'A number of students are absent' with 'The number of students is small'. After 'a number of' or 'a variety of', the verb follows the noun after 'of'; after 'the number of', the verb follows 'number'.

items.hint1: Find the true subject of the verb. Words that come between the subject and the gap can pull you the wrong way.
items.hint2: 'Each' refers to the candidates one at a time. In standard grammar, 'each' used as the subject takes a singular verb, even when a plural noun follows 'of'.
items.hint3: The phrase 'of the candidates' is not the subject. Say the sentence as 'Each ... required' and test which option sounds right with 'each' alone.
items.solution:
Answer: D. is

In standard grammar, 'each' used as a subject is singular, because it picks out the members of a group one at a time. The verb agrees with 'each', not with the plural noun inside 'of the candidates'.

How to tell: remove the phrase in the middle. 'Each of the candidates is required' becomes 'Each is required'. 'Each are required' is plainly wrong.

Why not the others:
A. are: this agrees with 'candidates', which is not the subject.
B. were: this is plural, and past tense as well.
C. have been: this is plural too.

Exam tip: with 'each of', 'every one of', 'one of' and 'neither of', cross out the 'of' phrase and make the verb agree with the first word.

items.hint1: Find the subject of the verb and ignore the phrase between it and the gap. Then decide whether the subject is singular or plural.
items.hint2: Some nouns end in s but take a singular verb. 'News' is one of them: we say 'the news is good', not 'the news are good'.
items.hint3: Replace the whole subject with 'it'. Which of the four options sounds right in 'it ... spread quickly'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. has

In modern English, 'news' is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb, even though it ends in s. So the verb must be singular: 'has spread'.

How to tell: replace 'the news of the team's victory' with 'it': 'It has spread quickly.' The phrase 'of the team's victory' only describes the news and does not change the verb.

Why not the others:
A. have: this is the plural form, used with 'they'.
B. are: this is plural, and 'are spread' is passive, which does not fit news spreading by itself.
D. were: this is plural, and past tense.

Exam tip: learn the common nouns that end in s but take a singular verb, such as news, mathematics, physics and measles. Replace them with 'it' to check the verb.

items.hint1: Look at the time phrase at the start of the sentence and at the word 'already'. Together they tell you when the ceremony starts compared with the arrival.
items.hint2: 'By the time we arrive' is about the future, because the arrival has not happened yet. So forms that describe the past do not fit.
items.hint3: 'Already' shows the ceremony begins before you arrive. Which future form shows an action that will be complete before another future event?
items.solution:
Answer: A. will have started

The future perfect tense (will have plus the past participle) is used for an action that will be complete before a certain point in the future. After 'by the time', English uses the simple present for the future event, here 'we arrive'.

How to tell:
'By the time we arrive' points to a future moment.
'Already' shows the ceremony starts before that moment.
Finished before a future point → future perfect: 'will have started'.

Why not the others:
B. would have started: this is used for imagined past situations, as in 'If we had left early, we would have seen it'; this sentence is about a real future event.
C. will start: this is the simple future and does not show that the start comes before the arrival, so it clashes with 'already'.
D. had started: this is the past perfect, which goes with a past event, as in 'By the time we arrived, the ceremony had started'.

Exam tip: match 'by the time' to the verb after it. 'By the time' plus a present verb usually takes will have plus the past participle; 'by the time' plus a past verb usually takes had plus the past participle.

items.hint1: All four options look alike, so compare them letter by letter. In long words, mistakes often hide in the doubled letters.
items.hint2: The correct spelling has a double c and a double m. Count the c's and the m's in each option.
items.hint3: Check the c's first, then the m's, and cross out any option that fails either count. Then look at the end of the option you have left: does 'date' there have a single t?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Accommodate

Accommodate is spelt with a double c and a double m: a-c-c-o-m-m-o-d-a-t-e. It is often misspelt because learners expect only one doubled letter.

How to tell: check the two doubled pairs, then the ending. Only one option has cc, mm and a single t.

Why not the others:
A. Accomodate: it has only one m.
C. Acommodate: it has only one c.
D. Accomodatte: it has only one m and a wrong double t at the end.

Exam tip: link a hard spelling to a memory aid. Accommodate is big enough to accommodate two c's and two m's. Committee, embarrass and occurrence also have more than one doubled letter.

items.hint1: The gap comes before 'their assignments'. Look at the time phrase and the word 'tomorrow' to decide when the action happens and whether it will be finished.
items.hint2: 'Tomorrow' puts the sentence in the future, so the choice is between future forms. 'By the time' asks whether the action will be finished before a certain point.
items.hint3: Between 'will complete' and 'will have completed', which one shows the work already done when the teacher comes to collect it?
items.solution:
Answer: B. will have completed

The future perfect tense (will have plus the past participle) shows an action that will be finished before a stated point in the future. 'By the time' with a future event is a strong signal for it.

How to tell:
'Tomorrow' puts the collecting in the future.
'By the time the teacher collects them' marks that future point.
The assignments are done before it → 'will have completed'.

Why not the others:
A. will complete: this says the work will happen in the future but not that it will be finished before the collection.
C. would complete: this is used for imagined situations or for a future seen from the past, as in 'He said they would complete it'; nothing here calls for that.
D. are completing: this is the present continuous and shows work in progress or a plan, not work finished before a point.

Exam tip: when a sentence has 'by the time', 'by then' or 'by next week' with a future event, will have plus the past participle is usually the form to choose.

items.hint1: Compare the options letter by letter. Think of a shorter word this one is built from, and how that word is spelt.
items.hint2: This word comes from 'conscience', which is 'con' plus 'science'. Check which options keep the letters 'sci' after 'con'.
items.hint3: Only two options begin 'consci'. Look at the letter just before 'ious' in each. Which ending matches words like 'cautious' and 'ambitious'?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Conscientious

Conscientious, meaning careful and hard-working, is built on 'conscience', which is 'con' plus 'science'. It keeps the 'sci' of conscience and ends in '-tious': con-sci-en-tious.

How to tell: check two points. The start must be 'consci', and the ending must be '-tious'. Only one option has both.

Why not the others:
B. Consciencious: it ends in '-cious' instead of '-tious'.
C. Consientious: it drops the c from 'sci'.
D. Concientious: it drops the s from 'sci'.

Exam tip: to spell a long word, find the shorter word inside it, such as conscience in conscientious, and keep that word's spelling. Then check the ending on its own.

items.hint1: Find the two time markers: a length of time, and a later event. Decide whether that later event is in the past, present or future.
items.hint2: 'Decided' is past tense, so the decision to move is in the past. The living went on for ten years before that past moment, so forms tied to now or to the future do not fit.
items.hint3: Two options use 'been living'. One links an action to now; the other links it to an earlier point in the past. Which one suits 'before we decided'?
items.solution:
Answer: A. had been living

The past perfect continuous tense (had been plus the -ing form) shows an action that went on over a period of time up to a moment in the past. 'For ten years' gives the period, and 'before we decided to move' gives the past moment.

How to tell:
'Decided' is past tense, so the end point is in the past.
The living went on for ten years before that point.
Continuing action up to a past point → 'had been living'.

Why not the others:
B. have been living: this is the present perfect continuous, which runs up to now, as in 'We have been living here for ten years'; it clashes with the past verb 'decided'.
C. are living: this is the present continuous and describes now, not the past.
D. will be living: this is future and cannot come before a past decision.

Exam tip: 'for' plus a length of time tells you the action lasted. Then look at the other verb: a past verb calls for had been plus -ing, while a link to the present calls for have been plus -ing.

items.hint1: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the same as the meaning of its separate words. Picture the scene the words describe, then ask what situation in life it stands for.
items.hint2: Options that simply describe eating take the words literally. An idiom's meaning is usually figurative, so set those aside.
items.hint3: Imagine taking a bite so big you cannot chew it. Of the two options left, which one is the same kind of mistake in daily life?
items.solution:
Answer: B. To take on more responsibility than one can handle

To bite off more than one can chew is an idiom meaning to agree to do more work, or take on a bigger task, than you are able to manage. The picture is of a mouthful too large to chew, and the task is like that mouthful.

How to tell: the key idea in the words is 'more than one can' manage. Only one option keeps that idea of too much.

Why not the others:
A. To eat too quickly: this reads the words literally, about food.
C. To speak without thinking: this is a different mistake, and nothing in the idiom is about speech.
D. To finish a meal completely: this is literal, and it is the reverse of having too much to manage.

Exam tip: in idiom questions, rule out any option that only repeats the literal picture, such as food, animals or buildings. Then pick the option that keeps the central idea of the picture.

items.hint1: A question tag is the short question added to the end of a statement. Look at the verb in the statement and whether the statement is positive or negative.
items.hint2: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag repeats the verb 'be' or the helping verb from the statement, not a new one.
items.hint3: The statement uses 'is', so the tags built on 'does' are out. Of the two left, which one matches a positive statement?
items.solution:
Answer: A. isn't he

A question tag repeats the helping verb, or the form of 'be', from the statement and reverses it: a positive statement takes a negative tag. The pronoun in the tag stands for the subject.

How to tell:
Verb in the statement: 'is' (is eager), and the statement is positive.
Tag: the negative form of 'is' → 'isn't'.
Subject 'the new employee' → 'he'.
So: 'The new employee is eager to learn the ropes, isn't he?'

Why not the others:
B. is he: this is positive, and a positive statement needs a negative tag.
C. doesn't he: 'does' is used when the statement has no helping verb or form of 'be', as in 'He works hard, doesn't he?'
D. does he: this uses the wrong verb and is also positive.

Exam tip: to form a tag, find the first helping verb or form of 'be' in the statement, flip it from positive to negative or back, and add the pronoun. Use do, does or did when the statement has no such verb.

items.hint1: Expand the short form at the start of the statement. Then check whether the statement is positive or negative.
items.hint2: 'You'd rather' stands for 'you would rather', so the tag uses 'would'. That rules out the tags built on 'did'.
items.hint3: Now look for the word 'not' in the statement. Does it make the statement positive or negative, and which kind of tag does that call for?
items.solution:
Answer: A. would you

A question tag repeats the helping verb of the statement and reverses it. In 'You'd rather not', 'you'd' stands for 'you would', and 'not' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive: 'would you'.

How to tell:
Expand the short form: 'You would rather not attend.'
Helping verb: 'would'.
The statement is negative, because of 'not'.
Negative statement → positive tag: 'would you?'

Why not the others:
B. wouldn't you: this is a negative tag, which would suit 'You'd rather attend', without 'not'.
C. did you: 'did' is the wrong helping verb. The short form 'd can stand for 'had' or 'would', but before 'rather' it is taken as 'would'.
D. didn't you: this has the wrong helping verb and is negative as well.

Exam tip: before choosing a tag, expand any short form ('d, 's, 've) and look for negative words such as not, never, hardly or nobody. They decide whether the tag is positive or negative.

items.hint1: This is an idiom, so its meaning is not the literal meaning of the words. Picture the scene and ask what it stands for.
items.hint2: Something kept inside a bag is suddenly let out where everyone can see it. The option that describes a real animal takes the words literally, so set it aside.
items.hint3: Think about what is 'in the bag' before it gets out: something kept out of sight. Test the remaining options against that idea.
items.solution:
Answer: B. To reveal a secret

To let the cat out of the bag is an idiom meaning to tell a secret, often by accident. The cat is the hidden thing, and once it is out of the bag it cannot be hidden again.

How to tell: the picture is of something kept out of sight coming out into the open. Only one option is about hidden information becoming known.

Why not the others:
A. To release a pet: this takes the words literally.
C. To solve a problem: nothing in the idiom is about finding an answer.
D. To create confusion: a secret coming out can cause trouble, but the idiom itself means revealing, not confusing.

Exam tip: learn idioms by their picture. Ask what is hidden, lost or gained in the scene; the meaning usually follows from that.

items.hint1: Idioms use an everyday picture to talk about something else. Ask what 'house' might stand for beyond a building.
items.hint2: Here 'house' stands for a person's own life and business, not a building. The phrase is often said to someone who should sort out their own problems first.
items.hint3: Cleaning and renovating are both things done to a building. Of the remaining two, which one is about a person's life rather than an event at home?
items.solution:
Answer: B. to organize one's personal affairs

To put one's house in order is an idiom meaning to sort out one's own affairs, such as work, money or behaviour, and fix one's own problems. 'House' stands for the person's life and business, not a building.

How to tell: the phrase is often used as advice, for example 'Before you criticise others, put your own house in order.' Only one option is about managing one's own life.

Why not the others:
A. to clean one's home thoroughly: this reads 'house' as a real building.
C. To renovate one's house: this is also literal, about repairing a building.
D. to host a house party: this is literal and has nothing to do with putting things in order.

Exam tip: when an idiom names an everyday object, such as a house, a bag or a boat, ask what it could stand for in a person's life. The literal options are usually the traps.

items.hint1: Use the rest of the sentence to work out the phrase. The word 'restricted' is a strong clue about what visitors could or could not do.
items.hint2: A restricted area is one where entry is limited. Options about cost or praise have nothing to do with entry, so set them aside.
items.hint3: Two options are left, and they mean opposite things. Which one agrees with the word 'restricted'?
items.solution:
Answer: C. prohibited or not allowed

Out of bounds means that people are not allowed to go into a place. 'Bounds' are limits or boundaries, so a place out of bounds lies outside the limits where you may go.

How to tell: 'restricted' means limited or controlled. A restricted area that is out of bounds for visitors is one that visitors are not allowed to enter.

Why not the others:
A. very expensive: the phrase is about entry, not price.
B. easily accessible: this is the opposite, and it clashes with 'restricted'.
D. highly recommended: this is about praise, not permission to enter.

Exam tip: when a phrase is used inside a sentence, look for a nearby word that points the same way, like 'restricted' here. The meaning you choose must agree with it.

items.hint1: Look at the last three words of the phrase. Ask what the word 'fault' usually means, and whether it is praise or criticism.
items.hint2: The phrase says the person is generous, so options saying they seldom give or give unwillingly do not fit.
items.hint3: Both remaining options say the person is very generous. Does 'fault' suggest the generosity is flawless, or that it goes too far?
items.solution:
Answer: C. excessively generous

Generous to a fault means generous to such a degree that it becomes a weakness, for example giving away so much that the person has too little left for themselves. 'To a fault' means too much, to the point of being a flaw, and it can follow other good qualities, as in 'honest to a fault'.

How to tell: a fault is a flaw or weakness. Generosity that reaches the point of a fault has gone too far, which is what 'excessively' means.

Why not the others:
A. rarely generous: the phrase says the person is very generous, not seldom generous.
B. perfectly generous: 'perfect' means without any fault, which is the reverse of 'to a fault'.
D. reluctantly generous: this means giving unwillingly, but the phrase describes someone who gives freely.

Exam tip: watch the small words that change a phrase's meaning. 'To a fault' after a good quality means 'too much', not 'perfectly'.

items.hint1: Say the given word aloud and listen only to the vowel sound in the middle. Do not trust the spelling: the same letters can stand for quite different sounds in English.
items.hint2: The vowel in bluff is the short sound you hear in cup and sun. All four options are spelt with ough, so say each one aloud. through ends with the long sound of too, so it does not match.
items.hint3: drought has the vowel of cow, so that leaves rough and cough. Say each of them straight after bluff and listen for the vowel of cup.
items.solution:
Answer: A. rough

The underlined u in bluff stands for the short pure vowel /ʌ/, the sound in cup and sun. In English the spelling ough is sounded in several different ways, so you have to match the sound, not the letters.

How to tell: rough is sounded /rʌf/, with the same /ʌ/ as bluff /blʌf/. The two words even rhyme.

Why not the others:
B. through: here ough is the long vowel /uː/ of too.
C. drought: here ough is /aʊ/, the gliding vowel of cow, not a short pure vowel.
D. cough: here ough is the short /ɒ/ of hot, made further back in the mouth with rounded lips.

Exam tip: when all the options share one spelling, such as ough or ea, the examiner is testing whether you listen or just read. Say each word in your head and compare it with an everyday word whose vowel you are sure of, such as cup, too, cow or hot.

items.hint1: Say weight aloud and listen to its vowel sound. Do not be guided by the spelling: letters such as ei and ea can each be sounded in more than one way.
items.hint2: The vowel in weight is the sound in late and day: it starts at e and glides towards i. beat has the long ee sound of see, so it does not match.
items.hint3: height has the vowel of high, so that leaves great and threat. Say both: which one sounds like late, and which like let?
items.solution:
Answer: B. great

The vowel in weight is the diphthong /eɪ/, the sound in day and late. A diphthong is a vowel that glides from one position to another inside one syllable. great is one of a small group of ea words, with break and steak, that are sounded /eɪ/.

How to tell: weight is /weɪt/ and great is /ɡreɪt/. They rhyme, so the vowel is the same.

Why not the others:
A. height: here eigh is /aɪ/, the vowel of high and my, even though it is spelt like weight.
C. beat: here ea is the long pure vowel /iː/ of see.
D. threat: here ea is the short pure vowel /e/ of bed and let.

Exam tip: the spellings ea and eigh each have more than one sound, so learn the odd ones in groups. great, break and steak have /eɪ/. head, bread and threat have /e/. weight, eight and neighbour have /eɪ/, but height has /aɪ/.

items.hint1: Say batch aloud and listen to the consonant sound at its end. Then notice that the letters ch are not sounded the same way in every word.
items.hint2: The end of batch is the sound at the start of chin, not a k sound. In many words that came into English from Greek, ch is sounded like k.
items.hint3: Say chemistry and chaos aloud: what sound does ch make in them? Now check the other two options the same way.
items.solution:
Answer: B. church

The tch in batch stands for /tʃ/, the sound at the start of chin. The letters ch often stand for this same sound, but in many words that came into English from Greek they stand for /k/.

How to tell: church begins and ends with /tʃ/, the same sound as the end of batch.

Why not the others:
A. chemistry: the ch is /k/, as in kit.
C. chaos: the ch is /k/, so it begins like cape.
D. ache: the ch is /k/, so the word rhymes with make.

Exam tip: ch in science words and other Greek words (chemistry, chorus, character, school, stomach, ache) is usually /k/. When a question asks for the /tʃ/ of chin, rule those out first, then say the rest aloud to be sure.

items.hint1: Say judge aloud and listen to its consonant sound. The letter g can stand for two different sounds, so say each option rather than trusting the letter.
items.hint2: The sound in judge is the one at the start of jam. The hard g of go is a different sound. Before a, o or u, the letter g is usually hard.
items.hint3: That leaves the two options where g comes before e or i. Say each one: which begins like jam, and which begins like get?
items.solution:
Answer: A. giant

The j and the dge in judge both stand for /dʒ/, the sound at the start of jam. The letter g can stand for this soft sound or for the hard sound /ɡ/ of go.

How to tell: giant is sounded /ˈdʒaɪənt/, so it begins with the same /dʒ/ as judge.

Why not the others:
B. gear: the g is hard /ɡ/, even though an e follows it.
C. gather: g before a is hard /ɡ/.
D. goal: g before o is hard /ɡ/.

Exam tip: g before a, o or u is usually hard, and g before e, i or y is often soft, but not always: gear, get, give and girl are hard. Use the next letter as a first guide, then say the word to be sure.

items.hint1: Break the word into its syllables and say it slowly, the way you would in normal speech. The stressed syllable is the one that sounds loudest and longest.
items.hint2: characterize is built from the noun character plus the ending -ize. Adding -ize usually does not move the main stress of the word it is added to.
items.hint3: The two middle syllables are weak and quick, so the choice is between the first syllable and the ending. Say character on its own, then add -ize without changing its rhythm.
items.solution:
Answer: A. CHARacterise

characterize is formed from character, which is stressed on its first syllable: CHAR-ac-ter. Adding the suffix (word ending) -ize usually leaves the main stress where it was in the base word, as in CRITicize from CRITic.

How to tell: say it in four syllables, CHAR-ac-ter-ize, /ˈkærəktəraɪz/. The first syllable is the loudest. The ending -ize has a full vowel and may carry a lighter, secondary stress, but not the main one.

Why not the others:
B. charACterise: ac is a weak syllable, sounded with the schwa /ə/, the short, relaxed uh sound.
C. characTERize: ter is also weak, sounded /tə/.
D. characterlZE: -ize carries at most a lighter stress, so putting the main stress there is a common mistake.

Exam tip: for a word ending in -ize or -ise, find the base word and its stress first, because the ending usually leaves it unchanged: CRITicize, SYMpathize, MODernize. The same check works for endings such as -ment and -ness: GOVernment, HAPpiness.

items.hint1: Split the word into its syllables and say it at normal speed. Listen for the one that is loudest and longest.
items.hint2: Stress can move when an ending is added. continent on its own is stressed on its first syllable, but adding -al changes the rhythm, so do not simply copy the stress of continent. The ending -al itself is weak.
items.hint3: Compare accident with accidental, and incident with incidental. Which of the two middle syllables of continental gets the push?
items.solution:
Answer: C. contiNENtal

Adding a suffix (word ending) can move a word's stress. CONtinent is stressed on its first syllable, but in continental the main stress moves to the syllable just before -al: con-ti-NEN-tal.

How to tell: say it at normal speed, /ˌkɒntɪˈnentl/. NEN is the loudest and longest syllable. CON keeps a lighter, secondary stress, which is why stressing it can sound possible.

Why not the others:
A. CONtinental: con carries only a secondary stress here, because the main stress it has in continent moves when -al is added.
B. conTInental: ti is a weak syllable with a short, light vowel.
D. continental: no syllable is marked in this option, and the final syllable, tal, is weak and cannot take the main stress.

Exam tip: words ending in -ental are stressed on the EN syllable: accidental, incidental, fundamental, environmental, experimental. When a noun takes the ending -al, check whether the stress has moved before you copy the noun's pattern.

items.hint1: Break the word into its syllables and say it as you would in a sentence. The stressed syllable is the loudest and longest.
items.hint2: Words ending in -ity follow one of the most regular stress patterns in English: the main stress falls on the syllable just before -ity, as in aBILity and elecTRICity. The ending itself is not stressed.
items.hint3: That leaves two candidates, IM and MU. Say immune on its own, then say immunity at normal speed. Does the syllable that is stressed in immune keep its push, or does the stress jump to the front?
items.solution:
Answer: B. imMUnity

Nouns ending in -ity are stressed on the syllable just before the ending. This is one of the most regular stress patterns in English, so the ending tells you where the stress goes.

How to tell: split the word as im-mu-ni-ty, sounded /ɪˈmjuːnəti/. The ending is -ity, and the syllable right before it is mu, so mu is stressed. It is also the stressed part of immune, imMUNE.

Why not the others:
A. IMmunity: im is a weak prefix here, said with a short, light vowel.
C. immuNIty: ni belongs to the -ity ending, which is not stressed.
D. immuniTY: the final ty is weak, like the end of city.

Exam tip: for a word ending in -ity, find the syllable just before -ity and stress it: aBILity, elecTRICity, comMUnity, uniVERsity.

items.hint1: In these questions, the word in capitals is the one being contrasted with something else. Ask yourself what the speaker is correcting or denying by stressing that word.
items.hint2: The stressed word here names a place. So the right option must be about a different place, not about who went or how they travelled.
items.hint3: Two options mention somewhere other than school. One gives another place they could have walked to instead; the other is about a different trip altogether. Which one sets up the contrast with where they went?
items.solution:
Answer: A. The children did not walk to the park

Emphatic stress marks the one word the speaker wants to contrast with something else. Stressing SCHOOL says the destination is the point: they walked to school, and not somewhere else.

How to tell: the stressed word names a place, so the implied meaning must deny another place as the end of that same walk. Only A does that: school, not the park.

Why not the others:
B. The children walked ; they didn't run: this contrasts walking with running, which would need the stress on WALKED.
C. Only the children went to school: this contrasts the children with other people, which would need the stress on CHILDREN.
D. The children didn't walk home: going home is a separate trip, so it does not give another place for the walk the sentence describes.

Exam tip: first ask what kind of word is stressed. A stressed place calls for a contrast of place, a stressed person for a contrast of person, and a stressed action for a contrast of action. Then choose the option that denies the other possibility for that same word.

items.hint1: The word in capitals is the one the speaker wants to set against something else. Work out what kind of word it is before you read the options.
items.hint2: The stressed word is the action. Two options change something other than the action, so they would need the stress on a different word.
items.hint3: Both remaining options involve a different action. One tells you what the speaker is saying did not happen; the other states a new fact that clashes with the sentence. Which one is the speaker implying?
items.solution:
Answer: A. My sister did not bake the cake

Emphatic stress on a verb contrasts the action with another action that someone might have expected. Stressing BOUGHT says she got the cake by buying it, not by making it herself.

How to tell: the implied meaning of a stressed word is what it rules out. The usual other way to get a cake is to bake it, so the stress implies that she did not bake it.

Why not the others:
B. My brother bought the cake: this changes the person, which would need the stress on SISTER.
C. My sister borrowed the cake: it changes the action, but it states a fact the sentence contradicts, while the stress implies what did not happen.
D. My sister bought the cookies: this changes the thing bought, which would need the stress on CAKE.

Exam tip: the meaning of emphatic stress is usually X, not Y. Reject options that change a word that was not stressed, then choose the one that denies the natural alternative to the stressed word.
